expectedText:
CONFIDENTIALITY OF MEDICAL INFORMATION ACT — EMPLOYER OBLIGATIONS — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Acme Corp.

EMPLOYER'S DUTY TO ESTABLISH CONFIDENTIALITY PROCEDURES
California Civil Code § 56.20(a) requires Acme Corp., as an employer that receives medical information about Jordan Lee, to establish appropriate procedures to ensure the confidentiality and protection of that information from unauthorized use and disclosure.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "Each employer who receives medical information shall establish appropriate procedures to ensure the confidentiality and protection from unauthorized use and disclosure of that information."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 56.20(a) (California Legislative Information text), Confidentiality of Medical Information Act — employer confidentiality-procedures duty (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=56.20.)
  Known gap: This is a single subdivision of one statutory section, Civil Code § 56.20(a). The statute names two non-exclusive examples of what such procedures 'may include' — instructing employees and agents who handle files on confidentiality, and security systems restricting access to files containing medical information — but does not mandate either specific measure, and its text does not itself require that medical information be kept on separate forms or in a file separate from the employee's regular personnel file (contrast the ADA confidentiality duty covered elsewhere in this corpus, which does require separate forms and files, and is a different, federal statute). This clause states the employer-specific duty in the Confidentiality of Medical Information Act's own employer chapter (Civil Code §§ 56.20-56.245); it does not restate a health care provider's, health care service plan's, or contractor's separate disclosure obligations under Civil Code § 56.10, which is a different audience addressed elsewhere in this corpus.

RESTRICTION ON AN EMPLOYER'S USE OR DISCLOSURE OF MEDICAL INFORMATION
California Civil Code § 56.20(c) provides that Acme Corp. may not use, disclose, or knowingly permit its employees or agents to use or disclose medical information that Acme Corp. possesses pertaining to Jordan Lee, without Jordan Lee first having signed an authorization under Civil Code § 56.11 or § 56.21 permitting that use or disclosure, except as specifically listed in the statute.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "No employer shall use, disclose, or knowingly permit its employees or agents to use or disclose medical information which the employer possesses pertaining to its employees without the patient having first signed an authorization under Section 56.11 or Section 56.21 permitting such use or disclosure, except as follows:"
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 56.20(c) (California Legislative Information text), Confidentiality of Medical Information Act — employer disclosure restriction (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=56.20.)
  Known gap: This is the introductory sentence of Civil Code § 56.20(c). The statute goes on to list four specific exceptions to this authorization requirement in paragraphs (1) through (4); one of them, the benefits-administration exception, is stated as its own clause elsewhere in this document (Civil Code § 56.20(c)(3) — a subdivision of this same statutory section, not an independent corroborating source). This document does not restate the other three listed exceptions (disclosure compelled by judicial or administrative process or other law; information relevant to a lawsuit, arbitration, or grievance between the employer and employee; and disclosure to a health care provider or professional to aid diagnosis or treatment when the patient cannot authorize it). As fetched, this provision's text applies to medical information the employer possesses 'pertaining to its employees'; it does not use the word 'applicant,' and this document does not independently verify that this specific provision, as opposed to some other part of the Confidentiality of Medical Information Act, extends to a job applicant who is not yet an employee. This is California law only; it does not describe any other state's employer medical-information rules.

PERMITTED USE FOR ADMINISTERING EMPLOYEE BENEFIT PLANS
One statutory exception to that authorization requirement is for benefits administration: Civil Code § 56.20(c)(3) provides that medical information pertaining to Jordan Lee may be used by Acme Corp. without an authorization only for the purpose of administering and maintaining employee benefit plans, including health care plans and plans providing short-term and long-term disability income, workers' compensation, and for determining eligibility for paid and unpaid leave from work for medical reasons.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "The information may be used only for the purpose of administering and maintaining employee benefit plans, including health care plans and plans providing short-term and long-term disability income, workers’ compensation and for determining eligibility for paid and unpaid leave from work for medical reasons."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 56.20(c)(3) (California Legislative Information text), Confidentiality of Medical Information Act — benefits-administration exception (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=56.20.)
  Known gap: This is paragraph (3) of the same subdivision addressed in another clause of this document, Civil Code § 56.20(c) — it is one of four listed exceptions within that subdivision, not an independent statutory section. This document does not restate the other three exceptions in § 56.20(c)(1), (2), and (4). Separately, Civil Code § 56.20(d), not quoted here, allows an employer to voluntarily narrow its own use or disclosure of medical information below what subdivision (c) otherwise permits, by a written agreement with an employee or a written company policy; that voluntary narrowing is not addressed by this clause. This clause states only that this use is permitted without an authorization for this stated purpose — it does not state that every other use or disclosure by an employer is prohibited, since the statute lists further exceptions this document does not repeat here.

NO DISCRIMINATION FOR REFUSING TO SIGN AN AUTHORIZATION
Civil Code § 56.20(b) provides that Jordan Lee may not be discriminated against in the terms or conditions of employment with Acme Corp. because Jordan Lee refused to sign an authorization under this part of the Confidentiality of Medical Information Act, although the statute does not prohibit Acme Corp. from taking action that is necessary in the absence of medical information caused by that refusal.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "No employee shall be discriminated against in terms or conditions of employment due to that employee’s refusal to sign an authorization"
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 56.20(b) (California Legislative Information text), Confidentiality of Medical Information Act — no discrimination for refusing to authorize (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=56.20.)
  Known gap: This is subdivision (b) of the same statutory section as the confidentiality-procedures duty and the disclosure restriction addressed in other clauses of this document, Civil Code § 56.20 — these are components of one section, not independent corroborating sources. This is a narrow anti-retaliation rule limited to the specific circumstance of an employee declining to sign an authorization under this part of the Act; it does not address retaliation for any other protected activity, and the statute does not itself define what employer action is 'necessary in the absence of medical information,' a phrase this document does not further interpret.

CIVIL PENALTIES AND A PRIVATE RIGHT OF ACTION FOR VIOLATIONS
Civil Code § 56.36 gives an individual a private right of action against a person or entity — which can include an employer — that negligently releases confidential medical information or records in violation of the Confidentiality of Medical Information Act, for nominal damages of $1,000 (without needing to prove actual or threatened damages) and for any actual damages sustained. The same section separately makes a person or entity that negligently discloses medical information in violation of the Act liable for an administrative fine or civil penalty of up to $2,500 per violation, and makes a person or entity, other than a licensed health care professional, that knowingly and willfully obtains, discloses, or uses medical information in violation of the Act liable for an administrative fine or civil penalty of up to $25,000 per violation.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "Except as provided in subdivision (e), nominal damages of one thousand dollars ($1,000). In order to recover under this paragraph, it is not necessary that the plaintiff suffered or was threatened with actual damages."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 56.36(b)(1) (California Legislative Information text), Confidentiality of Medical Information Act — private right of action, nominal damages (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=56.36.)
  "In addition, a person or entity that negligently discloses medical information in violation of the provisions of this part shall also be liable, irrespective of the amount of damages suffered by the patient as a result of that violation, for an administrative fine or civil penalty not to exceed two thousand five hundred dollars ($2,500) per violation."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 56.36(c)(1) (California Legislative Information text), Confidentiality of Medical Information Act — civil penalty for negligent disclosure (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=56.36.)
  "A person or entity, other than a licensed health care professional, who knowingly and willfully obtains, discloses, or uses medical information in violation of this part shall be liable for an administrative fine or civil penalty not to exceed twenty-five thousand dollars ($25,000) per violation."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 56.36(c)(2)(A) (California Legislative Information text), Confidentiality of Medical Information Act — civil penalty for knowing and willful violation (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=56.36.)
  Known gap: Civil Code § 56.36 is a general remedies section that applies to a violation of 'this part' — meaning any provision within the Confidentiality of Medical Information Act, Civil Code §§ 56-56.37 — and is not written as an employer-specific penalty provision; it reaches a violation of the employer-specific rules addressed elsewhere in this document, Civil Code § 56.20, only because § 56.20 sits within that same part. The four citations in this clause are all subdivisions of one statutory section, § 56.36: (b)(1) and (b)(2) together define the private civil action described in (b)'s introductory sentence (not separately quoted here), and (c)(1) and (c)(2)(A) are two separate, escalating civil-penalty tiers within the same subdivision (c) — none are independent sections corroborating each other. Section 56.36 contains substantial additional detail this clause does not restate: higher penalty tiers (up to $250,000 per violation) for knowing-and-willful violations done for financial gain, a list of factors used in assessing an administrative fine or civil penalty, an affirmative defense available to a covered entity or business associate that meets specified HIPAA-related conditions, and provisions on who may bring a civil-penalty action and how a recovered penalty is allocated between the state and local governments. This document does not evaluate whether any specific use or disclosure by an employer would actually violate the Act.

RECORD OF HOW MEDICAL INFORMATION IS HANDLED

Where the information is stored (e.g., separate file, restricted-access system): _______________________________________________
Persons or positions with authorized access: _______________________________________________
Stated purpose(s) for Acme Corp.'s use or disclosure of this information: _______________________________________________

SIGNATURE BLOCK
Signed at Sacramento, California on September 4, 2026.

_______________________________________________
Jordan Lee

_______________________________________________
For Acme Corp.
